paper_metadata.title: Socioeconomic variations in the course of stroke: unequal health outcomes, equal care?
paper_metadata.first_author: G A M van den Bos

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study uses a multicentre cohort from 23 randomly selected hospitals, providing a representative sample of hospitalised stroke patients in the Netherlands. Inclusion/exclusion and baseline characteristics are well-defined.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Patients were recruited from admissions to 23 randomly selected hospitals in the Netherlands.
items.reasoning: The source population is clearly defined as hospitalised stroke patients across a broad geographic range (23 hospitals).

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: All 760 patients were admitted within one week after stroke onset to 23 randomly selected Dutch hospitals.
items.reasoning: Random selection of hospitals and a clear timeframe for admission (within one week) minimize recruitment bias.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: While the follow-up duration (5 years) is mentioned, the specific calendar years of recruitment are not explicitly stated in the text.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: 23 randomly selected hospitals in the Netherlands.
items.reasoning: The setting (hospitals) and geographic location (Netherlands) are clearly specified.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: 465 patients were included who had had a stroke six months earlier... analyses necessarily were confined to the six months survivors.
items.reasoning: The study defines the 'zero time' for this analysis as 6 months post-stroke and specifies the exclusion of those who died before this point.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: Of the 502 patients who were still alive after six months, 17 patients refused to participate in the interview and for 20 patients socioeconomic status—that is, educational level—was unknown.
items.reasoning: The participation rate among eligible 6-month survivors is high (465/502 = 92.6%).

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Table 1 describes the characteristics of the patients in the study group by socioeconomic status.
items.reasoning: Table 1 provides a comprehensive list of age, gender, stroke severity, type, and recurrent stroke status.

quips_assessment.goal: Goal: To judge the risk of attrition bias (likelihood that relationship between PF and outcome are different for completing and non-completing participants).
quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: While mortality is high (expected in stroke), the authors explicitly addressed selective mortality by performing sensitivity analyses on 5-year survivors. However, detailed characteristics of non-mortality dropouts are sparse.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: The cumulative mortality was 34% at six months, 51% at three years, and 62% at five years.
items.reasoning: High attrition due to mortality is inherent to the condition, but it significantly reduces the sample size for long-term analysis.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text does not describe specific efforts to trace or collect data on those who refused or were lost for reasons other than death.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: 17 patients refused to participate... 20 patients socioeconomic status... was unknown... cumulative mortality was 34% at six months...
items.reasoning: The authors distinguish between refusal, missing data, and mortality.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The paper does not provide a comparison table between those lost to follow-up (non-deaths) and those who completed the study.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: The problem of the possible selective effect of socioeconomic status on mortality was tackled by repeating the analyses including only the survivors of five years after stroke.
items.reasoning: The authors acknowledge the potential for bias and attempt to control for it via sensitivity analysis, but do not definitively prove no difference exists for non-mortality dropouts.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Socioeconomic status (SES) is clearly defined by education level, a standard and stable metric for this age group. Measurement was consistent across the cohort.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: Socioeconomic status was assessed on the basis of educational level into two groups: (a) primary education or lower level secondary education, and (b) intermediate secondary or higher education.
items.reasoning: The prognostic factor (SES) is explicitly defined and categorized.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: education rather than income and occupation is considered to be a more stable indicator of lifelong socioeconomic status for the elderly
items.reasoning: The authors justify the use of education as a reliable proxy for SES in elderly populations.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: Socioeconomic status was assessed on the basis of educational level into two groups
items.reasoning: The cut-points for education levels are standard and not derived from the study's own data distribution.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Six months, three years, and five years after stroke, patients were interviewed at home.
items.reasoning: Standardized home interviews were used for all participants.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: for 20 patients socioeconomic status—that is, educational level—was unknown.
items.reasoning: Only 20 out of 502 survivors (approx 4%) had missing SES data, which is acceptable.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: For some of the remaining 465 patients, information on one or more of the other variables was missing.
items.reasoning: The study appears to use complete-case analysis rather than imputation for missing PF data.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Outcomes were measured using validated clinical scales (Barthel, Rankin) and standardized interviews, including proxy interviews to minimize bias from non-communicative patients.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: Disability in activities of daily living (ADL) was assessed with the Barthel Index... Handicap was measured with the modified Rankin Scale... Health perception was assessed with a single item question
items.reasoning: All three primary outcomes are clearly defined with their respective scales and follow-up intervals (6m, 3y, 5y).

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: Disability... was assessed with the Barthel Index... Handicap was measured with the modified Rankin Scale
items.reasoning: The study uses internationally recognized, validated instruments for stroke outcome assessment.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: patients were interviewed at home. If patients were not communicative... patient data were collected in a proxy interview
items.reasoning: The setting was consistent (home), and the use of proxy interviews ensured that the most severely affected patients were still measured, reducing bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study identifies and adjusts for major clinical and demographic confounders (age, gender, stroke severity/type) using multivariable logistic regression.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: The variables selected were age, gender, stroke type, stroke severity, and recurrent stroke.
items.reasoning: Key prognostic factors for stroke recovery were included in the model.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: Severity... was assessed with the Glasgow Coma Scale... Type of index stroke was subdivided into infratentorial strokes and supratentorial strokes
items.reasoning: Clinical confounders are defined using standard medical classifications.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Clinical data... were abstracted from the patients' medical and nursing hospital records.
items.reasoning: Data were sourced from objective medical records rather than patient recall.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Clinical data... were abstracted from the patients' medical and nursing hospital records.
items.reasoning: The abstraction process was uniform for the entire cohort.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: There is no mention of imputation; the study likely used available-case analysis.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The study did not use matching or stratification in the design phase; it relied on statistical adjustment.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: multivariate logistic regression analyses... adjusted for demographic and clinical variables.
items.reasoning: The analysis appropriately adjusted for the identified confounders.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical methods are appropriate for the longitudinal design. Results are reported with confidence intervals, and sensitivity analyses were performed to address potential biases.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: The effect sizes were expressed as odds ratios (ORs)... with 95% confidence intervals... All statistical analyses were performed with the statistical program SPSS 10.0.
items.reasoning: The strategy is transparently described, including the software used.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: In a previous study we found that these characteristics were major prognostic factors on health outcomes.
items.reasoning: Variable selection was based on prior empirical evidence and a clear conceptual framework (equity in health care).

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: multivariate logistic regression analyses using data six months, three years, and five years after stroke.
items.reasoning: Logistic regression is appropriate for the dichotomized outcomes used in the study.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Tables 2, 3, 4, and 5
items.reasoning: The authors report results for all time points and all outcomes, including non-significant findings.
